segments.line: You stir awake, and the room snaps into sharper focus.
Above each person's head, a small label floats,
a single word naming what sets off their allergies.
You notice a girl with pollen tagged above her,
the bus driver with cats, a construction worker with peanuts,
a jogger with pollen, a mother with dust.
You carry no label at all, just empty space above your own head.
The labels work on a simple rule. They appear the moment you notice a person
and hold steady while you look, then fade when you look away.
The label does not tell you how a person feels.
It only marks what triggers a reaction.
A pollen cloud, a cat's whisker,
a peanuts crumb, a dust moat,
each is a quiet identifier, not a judgment.
Seeing comes with a cost. Each label adds a faint pressure,
a soft whisper in your thoughts.
The more you read, the louder the hum grows.
You find yourself noticing the pollen drifting in the air.
The cats settled on the chair.
The peanuts left on the counter.
The dust settling in corners.
The world feels less open, more mapped with hidden prompts,
and yet you find yourself wondering. If you know what triggers someone,
can you protect them? Can you make different choices?
The tags are small, but they reshape how you move through any room.
You notice that friendships shift when you suddenly understand
why a colleague steps away from the office cat,
why a date chooses a peanut -free dessert,
why a classmate keeps tissue stocked.
The knowledge is quiet, but constant, a background hum that colors every interaction.
You find yourself glancing twice at the pollen in the spring air.
Twice at the cats on the sofa.
Twice at the peanuts at the potluck.
Twice at the dust in old books.
Each second look sharpens the sense
that the world is alive with hidden triggers.
What would your labels say?
